title: Enterprise Dedicated Intake: SLO translation, GPU-class mapping, and escalation playbook
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Problem statement: Enterprise sales and customer engineering teams are requesting clearer, repeatable guidance for converting customer SLAs and throughput asks into a deterministic dedicated capacity offer. Current intake is ad-hoc: engineers receive emails with vague throughput numbers, sales promise 'Xqps' without GPU-class context, and onboarding takes longer than expected. This ticket scopes a playbook and intake form that translates customer requirements (latency SLOs, peak tokens/sec, concurrency patterns, isolation needs, regulatory constraints) into: 1) recommended GPU class and node sizing, 2) reserved throughput targets and burst policies, 3) scaling policy templates (autoscale + warm pools + pre-warm windows), and 4) escalation and handoff runbooks for SLA exceptions.
acceptance_criteria: A consumable intake form (Google Form + Confluence template) capturing business and technical signals
SLO-to-capacity translation table that maps P50/P95/P99 latency SLOs and qps to GPU class recommendations (A100/H100/L4) and count ranges
A prioritization rubric (scorecard) that yields a numeric priority for dedicated onboarding requests
A scaling policy matrix with three templates: latency-first, cost-first, and availability-first
Escalation playbook documented with primary/secondary owners, SLAs for response, and communication templates
Sign-offs from Eng leads (Serving Runtime), Solutions Eng, and Legal for contract guardrails

notes: Key tradeoffs discussed: (1) conservative sizing reduces outage risk but increases cost of committed capacity; (2) allowing larger burst buckets improves UX but complicates billing and contract language; (3) per-customer quantization or lower-precision model variants can cut GPU requirements but may need QA on output quality. The playbook should default to conservative sizing for first 90 days, then permit right-sizing after telemetry-based evaluation.
playbook_highlights: Intake fields (minimum): business owner, contract value, peak tokens/sec, expected concurrency, workload type (chat/streaming/batch/embeddings), p99 latency SLO, data residency/regulatory needs, isolation requirement (shared vs dedicated VPC), preferred GPU families, acceptable model variants (fp16/int8), go-live date

Translation example: Customer reports 2000 concurrent chat sessions, average 40 tokens per response, 2 responses per session per minute. Sustained tokens/sec = (2000 * 40 * 2) / 60 = ~2667 tokens/sec. With 30% safety margin and expected KV cache hit rate 60%, reserved tokens/sec target = 2667 * 1.3 / 0.6 = ~5778 tokens/sec. Map this to GPU sizing using per-GPU throughput profiles (table in Confluence attachment).

GPU-class mapping guidance: latency-sensitive (<200ms p99) chat with long contexts => H100 preferred; general-purpose high-throughput generation => A100; cost-sensitive, smaller embedding workloads => L4 or T4 depending on model quantization. Always include fallback model variant list to enable graceful degradation.

Scaling templates: latency-first (tight p99 targets, scale aggressively at 60% capacity), cost-first (scale at 85% sustained, use warm pools for predictable spikes), availability-first (reserve 10% burst pool across nodes, pre-warm 30 minutes before business-critical windows).

Burst policy: define 'committed' vs 'burst' buckets on contract. Default burst allowance = 15% of committed throughput for 10 minutes; anything above triggers billing or throttling as per legal-approved template.

Escalation path: first response owner = Solutions Eng on-call (30 min), secondary = Runtime SRE (2 hours), executive escalation = Head of Customer Success for incidents impacting >2 customers or >24 hours.
